warmup.finding: Structured neuromuscular warm-ups (mixes of running, strength, balance, jumping and agility) cut injury rates in youth team sports by roughly a third to two-fifths.
warmup.dose: Typically 10-20 min, before practice, 2-3x/week across a season
warmup.effect: Lower-limb injury IRR 0.64 (25 studies, youth); adolescent team sports IRR 0.60 (40% fewer); 16 youth trials IRR 0.58

warmup.finding: Dose matters more than session length: two or three sessions a week gave the largest drop, and 10-15 minute sessions worked as well as longer ones. Programmes longer than 6 months were not better than shorter ones.
warmup.dose: 10-15 min per session, 2-3 sessions/week, more than ~30 min/week total
warmup.effect: 2x/week IRR 0.50; 3x/week IRR 0.40; 10-15 min IRR 0.55 vs longer 0.60

warmup.finding: The FIFA 11+ soccer warm-up lowers overall injury risk in recreational and sub-elite players; the older FIFA 11 did not show the same effect when pooled. Evidence in females is thinner than in males.
warmup.dose: Whole 11+ programme as the team warm-up
warmup.effect: FIFA programmes overall RR 0.75; FIFA 11+ alone IRR 0.61 (4 cluster RCTs)

warmup.finding: FIFA 11+ also lowered ankle injury rates in soccer (13-40 year olds) and ACL/knee injury in collegiate male soccer.
warmup.effect: Ankle injuries about 32% lower with 11+; knee injuries RR 0.42 and ACL RR 0.24 in male college soccer (NNT 70 for ACL)

warmup.finding: In youth basketball (11-18 y), a 10-minute coach-led neuromuscular warm-up (13 aerobic, agility, strength and balance exercises) was linked to 36% fewer ankle and knee injuries, and worked as well unsupervised as supervised.
warmup.dose: 10 min, 13 exercises, as the team warm-up

warmup.finding: A neuromuscular warm-up in adolescent male basketball (15 y average) roughly halved injury prevalence over three months; in pooled youth soccer and basketball data it cut ankle sprains about a third.
warmup.effect: Injury prevalence 10.9% vs 23.3%; ankle sprain IRR 0.68

warmup.finding: Compliance drives the effect: in adolescent female footballers the most compliant third had far fewer ACL injuries than the least compliant, and compliance fell month by month over the season.
warmup.effect: High-compliance tertile ACL RR 0.12 vs low-compliance; team compliance fell about 3% per month; time and motivation were the main barriers in elite handball

warmup.finding: Short static stretches cause only a small loss of strength and power, and the loss is smallest when each muscle is held 45 seconds or less. Static stretching alone should not be the whole warm-up.
warmup.dose: Keep static holds to 45 s or less per muscle within a fuller warm-up
warmup.effect: Strength -5.4%, power -1.9%, explosive performance -2.0% on average; larger losses with longer holds

warmup.finding: Stretching placed inside a warm-up that finishes with dynamic, sport-type activity has little effect on performance. Dynamic stretching gives small to moderate performance gains when done within minutes of activity; range-of-motion gains last under about 30 minutes.
warmup.effect: Static and PNF stretching showed no clear effect on all-cause or overuse injury

warmup.finding: Across 25 trials, stretching programmes did not prevent sports injuries, while strength training and balance/proprioception training did.
warmup.effect: Stretching RR 0.96 (no effect); balance training RR 0.55; strength training RR 0.32; overuse injuries RR 0.53

warmup.finding: Warming up in general improves performance in most outcomes tested, with little evidence of harm. A RAMP-style warm-up (raise, activate, mobilise, potentiate) beat static stretching and no warm-up for sprint and jump in youth soccer players.
warmup.effect: Warm-up improved performance in 79% of outcomes; RAMP vs static d=0.41, vs control d=0.52

warmup.finding: In male youth soccer, stretch-based warm-ups (static, dynamic, ballistic or PNF) gave no extra jump, sprint or kicking benefit over a standard warm-up.
Stretching increases joint range of motion over weeks, with static and PNF stretching beating dynamic; a single bout gives a small acute gain. Long-term static stretching lowers muscle stiffness.
warmup.effect: Chronic ROM ES about 1.0; acute ROM ES about 0.56; stiffness ES -0.75 after 3-12 weeks

warmup.finding: Stretching after exercise (cool-down) did not speed recovery of strength or reduce soreness compared with passive rest.
A coach-led warm-up targeting landing technique and trunk control (STOP-X, 8 weeks) improved jump-landing scores and lumbopelvic control in female basketball players who showed knee valgus.

Most combined warm-up and training programmes cut lower-limb injury and also improve sprint, jump and balance; recent syntheses repeat that dynamic warm-ups help acute sprint and jump while recovery evidence is mixed.

commonInjuries: Overuse shoulder pain in throwing athletes (handball, baseball, volleyball, softball, swimming)
Throwing-related rotator cuff and labral problems
Anterior dislocation/instability in contact sport
riskFactors: Weak external rotators and supraspinatus before the season
Low external/internal rotation strength ratio
Reduced total rotation range in the throwing shoulder
Obvious scapular dyskinesis
Throwing volume, pitching with fatigue or arm pain
Dominant arm, prior injury, older age in female overhead athletes
Excess abducted external rotation (in one cohort of left-handed high school pitchers)

riskReduction.finding: A coach-delivered shoulder programme added to the handball warm-up lowered shoulder problems in 660 elite players.
riskReduction.dose: 3x/week as part of the warm-up, 7-month season
riskReduction.effect: Shoulder problems 17% vs 23%; OR 0.72

riskReduction.finding: In elite handball, external rotation weakness, lower total rotation range and obvious scapular dyskinesis each predicted shoulder injury, which is why prevention targets those three things.
riskReduction.effect: Scapular dyskinesis OR 8.4; each 10 Nm more ER strength OR 0.71; each 5 degrees more rotation OR 0.77

riskReduction.finding: In professional pitchers, preseason weakness in external rotation and supraspinatus was associated with later throwing injury needing surgery.
A warm-up of stretching, mobility and balance drills cut shoulder and elbow injuries in 9-11 year old baseball players and raised ball speed.
riskReduction.effect: 1.7 vs 3.1 injuries per 1000 exposures (HR 1.94 for control)

riskReduction.finding: Pooled data did not find GIRD (loss of internal rotation) to be a statistically clear risk factor for upper-limb injury in overhead athletes; trends pointed the same way but crossed no-effect. Range-of-motion screening alone is a weak predictor.
Stretches and manual techniques for GIRD (sleeper stretch, cross-body stretch, joint mobilisation) improve range and pain, with no one method clearly better.

Volume and fatigue are the biggest modifiable shoulder/elbow risks in adolescent pitchers: injured pitchers threw more months, games, innings and pitches and more often pitched tired or in pain. Female overhead athletes show dominant-arm and volume as leading risks.
riskReduction.effect: Overuse/volume RR about 1.45 in female overhead athletes

riskReduction.finding: Thrower's Ten exercises improved upper-limb balance and explosive power in an RCT; the advanced version is described as a bridge from rehab to training for dynamic shoulder control.

returnToTraining.finding: Return to throwing after a shoulder or elbow injury is criteria-based: restore range, strength and scapular control first, then plyometrics, then an interval throwing programme that adds distance, effort and volume gradually.
returnToTraining.criteria: Normal ROM, strength and scapular mechanics, then plyometric progression, then interval throwing tracked by workload

returnToTraining.finding: A modern interval throwing programme for pitchers built on workload data runs about 217 days and keeps week-to-week workload change inside a 0.7-1.3 band far more of the time than the older programme.
returnToTraining.criteria: Gradual chronic workload build; acute:chronic ratio kept near 0.7-1.3

returnToTraining.finding: After surgical stabilisation for instability, about 7 in 10 return to their pre-injury level (Bankart or Latarjet), with lower rates in overhead athletes. Surgery and its timeline are a surgeon's decision.
Return to sport should be treated as a continuum running alongside rehab, not a single end-point test, and decided jointly by clinician, athlete and coach using risk and risk-tolerance reasoning.

commonInjuries: Medial elbow overuse in youth pitchers (including ulnar collateral ligament injury)
Lateral elbow tendinopathy (racket sports)
Throwing-related elbow pain requiring surgery in older adolescents
riskFactors: Pitching more than 100 innings a year
High pitch counts, many months of pitching, showcases
Pitching while fatigued or in pain
Also playing catcher (trend)
Higher pitch velocity
Coaches unaware of pitch-count guidance

riskReduction.finding: In a 10-year study of youth pitchers, those throwing more than 100 innings a year were about three and a half times more likely to be seriously injured.
riskReduction.dose: Cap innings below about 100 per year
riskReduction.effect: RR 3.5; cumulative injury 5%

riskReduction.finding: Adolescent pitchers who got hurt had pitched more and more often while tired; volume control and rest are the main levers.
riskReduction.dose: Limit pitches per game and per year, avoid year-round pitching, never pitch through fatigue or arm pain

riskReduction.finding: Many youth coaches do not track pitch counts by published guidance: over half were non-compliant and few could name overuse risk factors, so education is part of prevention.
A warm-up of stretching, mobility and balance work cut combined shoulder and elbow injuries in youth baseball.
riskReduction.effect: 1.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 exposures

riskReduction.finding: Elbow flexion during the pitch did not differ between youth pitchers with and without arm pain, so mechanics checks should look beyond that single angle.

For lateral elbow tendinopathy, eccentric wrist extensor exercise improves pain and strength and beats concentric exercise for pain; manual therapy plus eccentric training are the best supported physiotherapy options.
riskReduction.effect: Pain SMD -0.63, strength SMD 1.05 vs adjunct therapy alone

returnToTraining.finding: Non-operative care of ulnar collateral ligament injuries returns about 80% to sport; partial proximal tears do much better than distal ones. Grading and treatment choice belong to the treating clinician.
returnToTraining.criteria: Clinician decision; RTS 79.7%, proximal 89.7% vs distal 41.2%

returnToTraining.finding: After UCL reconstruction, most professional pitchers return to play in about a year, but return to the same level is lower and takes about 15 months.
Throwers return through a criteria-based sequence ending in an interval throwing programme, tracked by workload.
returnToTraining.criteria: Full ROM and strength, then plyometrics, then interval throwing

commonInjuries: Distal radial physeal stress injury ('gymnast's wrist') in skeletally immature gymnasts
Wrist sprains and fractures from falls (snowboarding, contact sport)
Scaphoid fracture
Triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) tears
Wrist and hand injuries in volleyball and tennis
riskFactors: Repeated weight-bearing through the hands in immature athletes
Age 10-14, higher skill level and more years of training in gymnastics
Falling onto an outstretched hand
High weekly training frequency and hours in tennis

riskReduction.finding: Wrist pain is very common in young gymnasts and tracks with radiographic physeal stress injury; pain was more common at ages 10-14 and with more training years.
riskReduction.effect: Wrist pain in 56% overall, 83% at age 10-14; about half had grade 2+ physeal stress

riskReduction.finding: Reviews of gymnast's wrist stress early recognition, load modification and attention to upper-limb weight-bearing volume, because long-term growth-plate damage can follow.
riskReduction.dose: Reduce hand weight-bearing load when pain appears

riskReduction.finding: Wrist guards roughly halve wrist injuries in snowboarders.
riskReduction.effect: OR 0.46; about 1 injury prevented per 50 riders

riskReduction.finding: In tennis, training three or more times a week or over 4.5 hours a week roughly doubled injury odds, and the wrist was the second most injured site.
riskReduction.effect: OR about 2.0-2.3 for higher training load

riskReduction.finding: In youth volleyball, the wrist, hand and fingers were the second most injured region after the ankle.
Grip-lock injuries in gymnasts link to excessive forearm flexion and wrist overpronation on bar swings; equipment fit and technique are the levers, but prevention evidence is limited.

returnToTraining.finding: After a scaphoid fracture managed without surgery, about 90% return to sport; return was much faster when sport in a cast was allowed (about 2 weeks) than when casting had to finish first (about 14 weeks). Fracture management is a clinician's decision.
After arthroscopic TFCC repair, about 84% return to work or sport, with range and grip usually back above 90% of the other side.
returnToTraining.criteria: Grip strength and ROM >90% of uninjured side

returnToTraining.finding: In professional athletes, hand and wrist injuries returned to play in about 2.8 months on average.

commonInjuries: Non-specific low back pain in adolescent athletes
Lumbar spondylolysis (pars stress fracture), especially with repeated extension and rotation
Lumbar bone stress injury in young cricket fast bowlers
riskFactors: Sport participation, high training volume/intensity
Concurrent lower-limb pain
Overweight/high BMI, older age
Low back extensor endurance
Previous low back pain or lumbar bone stress injury
Biological maturity and poor lumbopelvic control in fast bowlers

riskReduction.finding: Low back pain is common in adolescent athletes; risk rises with sport volume and intensity, lower-limb pain, high BMI and older age.
riskReduction.effect: 12-month prevalence 42%; 2-year incidence 11%

riskReduction.finding: Exercise combined with education is the best supported way to prevent a low back pain episode; exercise alone may also help.
riskReduction.effect: Exercise + education RR 0.55; exercise alone RR 0.65

riskReduction.finding: Exercise programmes lower future back pain intensity, and exercise with education lowers future disability.
riskReduction.effect: Pain MD -4.5; disability MD -6.3 (0-100 scales)

riskReduction.finding: Low isometric back extensor endurance (Biering-Sorensen hold) predicted first-time low back trouble in men; good endurance appeared protective.
Athletes with a history of low back pain show lower trunk extensor endurance and extension torque, supporting endurance work in prevention.
riskReduction.effect: Large negative correlation between extensor endurance and disability (r=-0.79)

riskReduction.finding: In young cricket fast bowlers, lumbar bone stress injury is common and tied to prior injury and maturity; workload regulation, technique screening and lumbopelvic strengthening are the recommended levers.
riskReduction.effect: Seasonal prevalence 16.3%

returnToTraining.finding: Most elite athletes with active spondylolysis returned to the same level within about 5.5 months of conservative treatment; healing was most likely with a unilateral lesion.
returnToTraining.criteria: Clinician-led diagnosis, imaging and bracing decisions

returnToTraining.finding: In children, early-stage spondylolysis healed in almost all cases within about 2.5 months of conservative care; healing was lower at later stages and recurrence was about 26%.
returnToTraining.criteria: Stage on imaging decides plan; clinician decision

returnToTraining.finding: Simple exam tests are not reliable enough to diagnose spondylolysis in athletes with back pain, so suspected pars injury in a young athlete needs clinical assessment and imaging.

commonInjuries: Hamstring strain (sprinting)
Adductor-related groin pain
Acute adductor muscle injury
Iliopsoas, inguinal, pubic and hip-related groin pain
riskFactors: Previous hamstring, ACL or calf injury
Older age
Low eccentric hamstring strength and high-speed running exposure
Previous groin injury
Low adductor strength, absolute and relative to abductors
Higher level of play, lower sport-specific training
Reduced hip rotation range

riskReduction.finding: Programmes that include the Nordic hamstring exercise roughly halve hamstring injuries across sports.
riskReduction.effect: RR 0.49 overall; 0.52 in RCTs only

riskReduction.finding: A progressive eccentric programme in men's soccer cut new and especially recurrent hamstring injuries; amateur soccer RCT agreed.
riskReduction.dose: 10-week progressive build then a weekly in-season dose (Petersen); 25 sessions over 13 weeks (van der Horst)
riskReduction.effect: Overall RR 0.29, recurrent RR 0.14, NNT 13; amateur OR 0.28

riskReduction.finding: Eccentric training reduced hamstring injury 57-70% across RCTs; low-volume Nordic programmes gave strength gains as large as high-volume ones after 6+ weeks, and high volumes caused more soreness, which hurts compliance.
riskReduction.dose: Low volume is enough after at least 6 weeks
riskReduction.effect: Eccentric strength g about 2.1-2.3 for both volumes

riskReduction.finding: Recent hamstring injury, any history of it, older age and prior ACL or calf strain raise hamstring risk.
riskReduction.effect: Recent HSI RR 4.8; any history RR 2.7; prior ACL RR 1.7

riskReduction.finding: A single-exercise adductor programme (Copenhagen adduction with three levels) cut groin problems by about 40% in male footballers.
riskReduction.dose: 3x/week for 6-8 weeks preseason, then 1x/week in season
riskReduction.effect: Prevalence 13.5% vs 21.3%; OR 0.59

riskReduction.finding: Eight weeks of the Copenhagen adduction exercise in season raised eccentric adductor strength by about 36% with high compliance and little soreness.
riskReduction.effect: +35.7% eccentric adduction strength

riskReduction.finding: Previous groin injury, higher level of play, weaker adductors and less sport-specific training are associated with groin injury; screening tools such as hamstring:quadriceps ratio and hip abduction range have some predictive value.
Interventions including the Nordic, FIFA 11+ and core/balance work reduced hamstring injuries in professional and semi-professional football.
riskReduction.effect: IRR 0.44

returnToTraining.finding: Hamstring rehab is mostly progressed by pain; clearance usually uses clinical exam and performance tests. Protocols using the Askling H-test had the lowest re-injury rates.
returnToTraining.criteria: Pain-guided progression; clinical tests, strength and sprint tests

returnToTraining.finding: A lengthening-focused hamstring rehab protocol returned elite footballers about three weeks faster than conventional exercise; starting lengthening work earlier did not speed return further.
After acute adductor injuries in male athletes, criteria-based rehab got grade 0-2 injuries pain-free in about 13 days and back to full team training in about 18 days.
returnToTraining.criteria: Pain-free clinical tests, completed controlled sport training, then full team training

returnToTraining.finding: Groin pain should be classified clinically (adductor-, iliopsoas-, inguinal-, pubic- or hip-related) before rehab is planned; that classification is a clinician task.
Athletes with longstanding groin pain show lower adductor squeeze values and reduced hip range, so squeeze strength is a useful rehab marker.

commonInjuries: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture, highest in adolescent females
Patellofemoral pain
Osgood-Schlatter (tibial tubercle apophysitis) in growing athletes
Patellar tendinopathy
riskFactors: Knee abduction (valgus) angle and moment on landing, higher landing force
Female sex for non-contact ACL
Quadriceps weakness (patellofemoral pain in military); hip weakness in adolescents not consistently a risk
Younger age and high activity for second ACL injury
Early return to sport and quadriceps asymmetry after ACL surgery

riskReduction.finding: ACL prevention programmes halve ACL injuries in athletes overall and cut non-contact ACL injuries by two-thirds in females; evidence in males is insufficient.
riskReduction.effect: All ACL OR 0.50; female non-contact OR 0.33

riskReduction.finding: In young females, neuromuscular training cut ACL risk from 1 in 54 to 1 in 111, and middle/high school programmes worked better than college/pro ones.
riskReduction.effect: OR 0.51; school-age OR 0.38

riskReduction.finding: Female athletes who later tore an ACL landed with more knee abduction and much higher abduction moments; programmes should train the frontal plane, not only knee bend.
riskReduction.effect: Knee abduction moment 2.5x higher; predicted injury 78% sensitivity, 73% specificity

riskReduction.finding: Youth neuromuscular warm-ups reduce lower-limb injury, with a protective trend for the knee; youth basketball cut knee and ankle injury 36%.
riskReduction.effect: Lower-limb IRR 0.64; knee IRR 0.74 (not significant); basketball knee+ankle IRR 0.64

riskReduction.finding: Compliance decides results: highly compliant adolescent female footballers had 88% fewer ACL injuries.
Quadriceps weakness predicted patellofemoral pain in military recruits; age, height, weight, BMI and Q angle did not. Squats load the patellofemoral joint most between 60 and 90 degrees of knee bend.
riskReduction.effect: Quadriceps weakness SMD -0.69

riskReduction.finding: Osgood-Schlatter is mostly self-limiting; reviews suggest quadriceps and hamstring flexibility work and load management at sensitive ages, but prevention trials are lacking.

returnToTraining.finding: After ACL reconstruction, waiting until at least 9 months and having symmetrical quadriceps strength cut reinjury: risk fell 51% for each month return was delayed up to 9 months, and returning to pivoting sport raised risk 4-fold.
returnToTraining.criteria: At least 9 months after surgery; quadriceps LSI near symmetry; passing RTS battery

returnToTraining.finding: Professional athletes who did not meet all six discharge criteria (isokinetic strength, running agility, hop tests) had four times the graft rupture risk; a lower hamstring:quadriceps ratio also raised risk.
returnToTraining.criteria: Six criteria incl. strength and single, triple and crossover hop tests

returnToTraining.finding: Only about 23% of patients pass full RTS test batteries; passing lowered graft rupture risk but did not clearly lower all subsequent ACL injuries.
returnToTraining.criteria: Test batteries help but do not guarantee safety

returnToTraining.finding: Typical phase goals are a quadriceps and hop LSI of 85%+ before agility and sprinting, and 90%+ with no pain or swelling and assessed confidence before full return.
returnToTraining.criteria: LSI >=85% mid-phase, >=90% at clearance; no effusion; psychological readiness

returnToTraining.finding: Hop symmetry often passes while quadriceps symmetry is still under 90%, so strength must be measured, not inferred from hops.
Young athletes face high second-ACL rates: about 23% for under-25s who return to sport, and 27% for female soccer players.
Psychological readiness (ACL-RSI) rises from 6 to 12 months in adolescents and predicts return; knee confidence and limb symmetry relate to readiness.
Rehab protocols in soccer vary widely, and many studies use only one or two test batteries; the surgeon and therapist own the timeline.

commonInjuries: Lateral ankle sprain, the most common sport injury in many court and field sports
Recurrent sprain and chronic ankle instability
Achilles and patellar tendinopathy in adolescents (Achilles less common)
riskFactors: Previous ankle sprain (about 2-3x risk)
Basketball vs soccer
In males: higher BMI/weight, weaker hip abduction, poorer dynamic balance
In females: weaker dorsiflexion strength
Female sex and younger age have higher incidence

riskReduction.finding: Proprioceptive/balance training reduces ankle sprains by about a third, both for first sprains and repeats.
riskReduction.effect: RR 0.65 overall; 0.64 with prior sprain; NNT 17

riskReduction.finding: A balance programme in high school soccer and basketball cut ankle sprains, with the largest benefit in those with a past sprain.
riskReduction.effect: 1.13 vs 1.87 sprains per 1000 exposures; RR 0.56

riskReduction.finding: Unsupervised home balance-board training after a sprain cut recurrences by about 35%.
riskReduction.dose: Done at home after usual care (12-70 year olds)
riskReduction.effect: 22% vs 33% recurrence; RR 0.63; NNT 9

riskReduction.finding: Lace-up ankle braces cut acute ankle injuries by about two-thirds in high school basketball, with or without a past injury.
Previous sprain doubles to triples risk, and risk factors differ by sex (hip abduction strength and balance in males; dorsiflexion strength in females).
riskReduction.effect: Prior sprain OR 2.74

riskReduction.finding: Neuromuscular warm-ups including FIFA 11+ reduce ankle sprains in youth soccer and basketball.
riskReduction.effect: Youth ankle sprain IRR 0.68; FIFA 11+ about 32% fewer ankle injuries

riskReduction.finding: Females and younger athletes have the highest sprain incidence, so prevention should start early.
riskReduction.effect: Females 13.6 vs males 6.9 per 1000 exposures

riskReduction.finding: Tape and braces restrict inversion; semirigid braces restrict more after exercise. They did not improve proprioception in unstable ankles, and guidelines favour braces for preventing recurrence.

returnToTraining.finding: Exercise-based rehab after an acute sprain cuts reinjury, but the best content and dose are not settled.
An international consensus (PAASS) sets five domains for return after a lateral ankle sprain: Pain, Ankle impairments, Athlete perception, Sensorimotor control and Sport/functional performance.
returnToTraining.criteria: Pain in sport and over 24 h; ROM, strength, endurance, power; confidence; balance; hops, agility, full session

returnToTraining.finding: Clinical guidelines favour supervised exercise over passive treatment, reserve surgery for failed rehab and suggest braces to prevent recurrence. Suspected fracture or severe sprains need a clinician.
Ongoing instability after a sprain needs assessment because chronic instability can follow; evaluation in the subacute and return phases should look for those deficits.

commonInjuries: Sport-related concussion
Cervical spine injury in collision sports (tackling, scrums)
Neck strain
riskFactors: Lower overall neck strength (high school athletes)
Collision sport, bodychecking in youth hockey
No mouthguard in collision sports
Illegal or unsafe technique in tackling and scrummaging

riskReduction.finding: In high school athletes, each extra pound of neck strength lowered concussion odds by about 5% after adjusting for sex and sport.
riskReduction.effect: OR 0.95 per lb

riskReduction.finding: A coach-delivered pre-activity programme (balance, whole-body resistance including neck work, plyometrics, landing and cutting) in schoolboy rugby lowered concussion, and teams doing it 3+ times a week saw large drops in all match injuries.
riskReduction.effect: Concussion RR 0.71 overall; with 3+/week RR 0.41 concussion and 0.28 all match injury

riskReduction.finding: Neck strengthening in male rugby players was linked to 45% fewer concussions in pooled data, though only two studies measured it.

Five weeks of neck strength training raised isometric neck strength in every direction in rugby players; reviews confirm isometric routines raise strength, though direct concussion evidence is limited.
riskReduction.effect: Flexion about 334 to 396 N; extension 606 to 734 N

riskReduction.finding: Mouthguards in collision sport and banning bodychecking in youth hockey lower concussion; the paediatric consensus also lists neuromuscular training in adolescent rugby.
riskReduction.effect: Mouthguard IRR 0.74; no-bodychecking about 58% fewer concussions

riskReduction.finding: Cervical spine injury prevention in collision sport rests on rules, safe technique coaching (tackling, scrummaging) and education.

returnToTraining.finding: For children and adolescents, early return to light activity and less screen time help recovery more than strict rest; cervicovestibular rehab is advised if dizziness, neck pain or headache last over 10 days. Diagnosis and clearance are a clinician's job.
The 6th international concussion consensus (Amsterdam 2022) provides the current assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6) and management principles.
returnToTraining.criteria: Use consensus tools under medical supervision

placement.finding: Doing the Nordic hamstring exercise before soccer training left the hamstrings weaker eccentrically during later football exercise than doing it after; the authors warn pre-training Nordics may add risk.
placement.effect: Eccentric peak torque 14-19% lower during simulated play when done beforehand

placement.finding: Over 12 weeks, Nordics done before or after training gave the same strength gain; muscle structure changes differed (longer fascicles when done before, thicker muscle when done after).
Eccentric hamstring work done after soccer training gave better protection of eccentric strength late in a match simulation than the same work in the warm-up.
Match-like fatigue lowers the hamstring eccentric:quadriceps concentric strength ratio by about 10%, matching the late-half rise in hamstring strains.
Fatigue changes landing mechanics, but most measures conflict across studies; reviews call for more research before changing ACL programmes for fatigue.
Warm-up-based programmes (FIFA 11+, SHRed Basketball, ACL programmes) are proven in the warm-up slot; short 10-15 min doses 2-3 times a week are effective there.
